newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: McCreevy to take control of Ireland's purse strings.
newsitem.headline: McCreevy to take control of Ireland's purse strings.

text.p: Not content to simply inherit a booming economy, Ireland's new finance minister, Charlie McCreevy, has set himself the tough task of reining in public spending, a feat that eluded his predecessor.

The tough-talking 47-year-old Kildare accountant, who hounded the previous government for their "spend, spend and spend again approach", has vowed to keep increases in public expenditure to a nominal four percent a year.
"The increase in spending will be four percent and if inflation is five percent for the lifetime of the government, then there would have to be a real decrease in spending," he said recently.
"The four percent was put there deliberately by us in order that there could be no fudging. This is an exact science."
McCreevy's long-standing commitment to controlling government spending is not in doubt.

In 1982, he found himself briefly expelled from Fianna Fail for his persistent demands for fiscal rectitude which was seen as a criticism of the party leadership under former prime minister Charles Haughey.

While serving as Minister for Social Welfare, McCreevy introduced a raft of cuts known as the "dirty dozen" which included ending disability and dental benefit for people unemployed for more than four years and cutting assistance on electricity and gas bills.
This, and his shake up of Bord Failte, the Irish Tourist Board, during a spell as Minister for Tourism and Trade have copper fastened his reputation as a man of serious fiscal rectitude.
"He is conservative on financial matters and can be expected to keep a tight grip on the nation's purse strings," one commentator said of him.
But analysts say he will face a tough task if he is to meet his demanding four percent target.

"The old administration limited real spending growth to four percent and failed spectacularly to meet their target. To keep nominal spending growth to four percent would be an extraordinary achievement if he managed it," one economist said.
Aside from the fiscal challenge he has set himself, McCreevy will be the envy of his EU counterparts as he inherits the fastest growing economy in the European Union.
Dubbed the "Celtic Tiger", Ireland's inflation rates remain at German levels while the economy has enjoyed an Asian-style growth rate of 25 percent over the last three years.
Analysts say the only cloud on the horizon is the recent weakness of the Irish pound which could threaten Ireland's low inflation rate and put upward pressure on interest rates.
Recent market speculation has focused on the possibility that the new government will revalue the punt but whatever McCreevy decides to do, he will be careful about what he says.
He recently told outgoing Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn he had made "a grave error" after comments by Quinn triggered selling pressure on the punt.
"I accept that anybody can make an error in an off-the-cuff remark, but regarding currency matters, I can say that a shut mouth is often the very best policy."

While Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern has voiced his commitment to Ireland joining the European Monetary Union, the outspoken McCreevy has been more open about the problems facing Ireland if Britain remains outside the single currency.
"Lets be honest about it, if Britain is staying out there are going to be problems," he told the Irish Times in April.
"Even though we have reduced our dependence on trade with Britain, it still is, and always will be, our major trading partner."

McCreevy lands one of the top jobs in Irish politics after weathering a disappointingly chequered 20 years in politics sometimes favoured, sometimes shunned, often hampered by his lack of adherence to "club rules".
A racing enthusiast, McCreevy backed a hunch in 1991 and supported the challenger, Albert Reynolds, for the leadership, a move which rescued him from a decade of backbench wrangling.
When Reynolds became Prime Minister, he rewarded him with the post of Minister for Social Welfare.

The fall of Albert Reynolds Fianna Fail/Labour coalition in 1994 and the accession of Bertie Ahern as a "consensus" party leader resulted in a surprise promotion for McCreevy to Fianna Fail's spokesman on finance.
